# How to use this guide

Community Health Nursing I (N-COMH(I)310) is studied in Semester 5 alongside Child Health Nursing and Mental Health Nursing. It is the first systematic study of public health nursing in the B.Sc Nursing programme, shifting focus from the individual patient in a hospital to the community as the client. The subject covers environmental health, nutrition, health education, epidemiology, communicable disease programmes, and non-communicable disease programmes. Because India's national health programmes are examined directly, this subject requires you to know programme names, targets, key interventions, and implementing agencies alongside theoretical concepts.

## Exam pattern

N-COMH(I)310 is examined at the end of Semester 5 as a **standalone theory paper** following the standard INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing exam format.

**Typical INC B.Sc Nursing end-semester theory paper (75 marks, 3 hours)**

| Section | Type | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 20 objective questions (MCQ or fill-in-the-blank) — attempt all | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 questions | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 questions | 7 × 5 = 35 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

Confirm the exact format with your college; some universities use slightly different section patterns.

## How the unit files are arranged

The INC 2021 syllabus for N-COMH(I)310 has eight numbered units. This pack keeps **one notes file per INC unit**, with unit numbers matching directly.

| Notes file | INC unit | Key topics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 — Community health concepts | I + II | Definitions, Bhore Committee, WHO definition of health, determinants, levels of prevention, PHC elements, delivery system in India |
| Unit 2 — Environmental health | III | Air/water/soil pollution, water treatment, sanitation, latrine types, solid and biomedical waste, vector control, Swachh Bharat Mission |
| Unit 3 — Nutrition | IV | ABCD assessment, PEM classification (marasmus/kwashiorkor), SAM management, national nutrition programmes (ICDS, MDMS, Poshan Abhiyaan), food-borne diseases, food safety (FSSAI, COTPA) |
| Unit 4 — BCC and health education | V | Principles of health education, BCC vs IEC, Health Belief Model, Transtheoretical Model, Social Cognitive Theory, communication methods, home visit, bag technique, community diagnosis |
| Unit 5 — Family health, PHC, records | VI | Family assessment, ANC standards, immunisation schedule, cold chain, school health services, PHC infrastructure (SC/PHC/CHC/HWC), ASHA, MCH records, IHMP/MCTS |
| Unit 6 — Epidemiology | VII | Rates (IMR, MMR, CDR), incidence vs prevalence, study designs, Bradford Hill criteria, screening (sensitivity/specificity), IDSP, outbreak investigation (epi curve, attack rate) |
| Unit 7 — Communicable diseases | VIII | TB/NTEP/DOTS, malaria/NVBDCP/ACTs, dengue, filaria/MDA, kala-azar, HIV/NACP, cholera, typhoid, rabies, JE |
| Unit 8 — NCDs | IX | Hypertension, diabetes, CVD, stroke, cancer screening (VIA, CBE), COPD, NPCDCS, tobacco control (NTCP/COTPA), mental health (NMHP/DMHP) |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Know the programme names and their acronyms.** The examiner will award marks for correctly naming programmes: "NVBDCP" scores marks that "vector control programme" does not. Learn at least the full name and acronym of each national programme.

2. **Link disease → route of transmission → national programme → nurse's role.** For any communicable disease question, structure your answer as: causative agent → transmission route → clinical features → diagnosis → treatment → national programme → nursing care. This format reliably scores 7–8 marks on a 10-mark essay.

3. **Epidemiology formulas need to be learned precisely.** The examiner expects the correct formula with the denominator clearly stated. IMR = Deaths under 1 year ÷ Live births × 1,000. Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN). Write the formula first, then give the clinical meaning.

4. **For NCD questions, include risk factors and primary prevention.** An answer about hypertension or diabetes that only describes clinical management misses the community nursing dimension. Always state: lifestyle interventions (diet, exercise, smoking cessation, salt reduction), screening approach, and adherence support.

5. **BCC models often come as 10-mark or 5-mark questions.** For a Health Belief Model question, name all six constructs with an example for each. For the Transtheoretical Model, name all five stages and the matching communication strategy.

6. **Outbreak investigation steps are listed in order.** The examiner expects the steps in sequence. Memorise: Verify → Confirm → Define case → Count → Descriptive epi → Hypothesise → Test → Control → Communicate → Report.

7. **For food-borne disease questions**: give the organism, incubation period, source, clinical features, and control measures. Know the classic scenario: staphylococcal food poisoning has a very short incubation (2–6 hours) and is caused by pre-formed toxin in food left at room temperature — antibiotics are not indicated.

8. **School health services are regularly asked as a 5-mark or 10-mark question.** Use the five components: health appraisal, health promotion, communicable disease control, healthy environment, and special services (nutrition, mental health).

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most years; commit the full answer to memory.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a broader question.
- **Low** — appears rarely; useful for MCQs and to round off a long essay.

These ratings are estimates based on INC syllabus weightings and common exam patterns. They are a guide, not a guarantee.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | High-probability topics |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Community health | Levels of prevention, PHC principles and elements (Alma-Ata), Bhore Committee, rural health infrastructure (SC/PHC/CHC) |
| 2 Environmental health | Vector control (malaria mosquito types and control), water quality parameters, water treatment steps, biomedical waste colour coding |
| 3 Nutrition | ABCD nutritional assessment, kwashiorkor vs marasmus (table), SAM management (F-75/F-100/RUTF), ICDS components |
| 4 BCC | Health Belief Model (name and explain all 6 components), Transtheoretical Model (stages of change), home visit bag technique |
| 5 Family/PHC/records | Immunisation schedule (know all vaccines at each age), cold chain equipment, ASHA roles, school health services components |
| 6 Epidemiology | IMR definition and formula, incidence vs prevalence (table), sensitivity vs specificity, outbreak investigation steps in order, epi curve interpretation |
| 7 Communicable diseases | TB (DOTS, drug regimen), malaria (types, treatment ACT/chloroquine), dengue (features, no antibiotics), HIV NACP activities |
| 8 NCDs | Hypertension definition and lifestyle management, diabetes screening and foot care, cervical cancer VIA screening, NPCDCS activities |

# Last-night revision sheet

Print this, fold it, carry it to the exam hall. These are the numbers, sequences, and comparisons that appear as MCQs and short answers every year.

---

## Key numbers to memorise

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Sub-Centre covers population (plain) | 3,000–5,000 |
| PHC covers population (plain) | 20,000–30,000 |
| CHC covers population | 80,000–1,20,000 |
| Minimum ANC visits (NHM India) | 4 (WHO recommends ≥ 8) |
| PNC home visits (national standard) | ≥ 3 (within 24 h, Day 3, Day 7) |
| Exclusive breastfeeding duration | 6 months |
| Breastfeeding continuation target | Up to 2 years + |
| IMR (India 2022, approx) | ~27 per 1,000 live births |
| MMR (India 2018–20, SRS) | 97 per 100,000 live births |
| WHO definition of health | Complete physical, mental, and social well-being — not merely absence of disease |
| Alma-Ata elements of PHC | 8 (education, food/nutrition, water/sanitation, MCH/FP, immunisation, endemic disease control, essential drugs, common disease treatment) |
| Swachh Bharat Mission target year | ODF India declared October 2019 |
| TB elimination target (India) | 2025 (< 1 case per million) |
| Kala-azar elimination target | < 1 case per 10,000 at block level |
| DOTS stands for | Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course |
| NTEP standard TB treatment | 2HRZE + 4HR (6 months) |
| Malaria: P. vivax radical cure | Chloroquine 25 mg/kg over 3 days + Primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day × 14 days |
| Malaria: P. falciparum treatment | ACT (Artesunate + Sulphadoxine-Pyrimethamine, 3 days) |
| DEC + Albendazole MDA (filaria) | Annual × 5 years to interrupt transmission |
| National Deworming Day | 10 February and 10 August; Albendazole 400 mg for 1–19 years |
| VIA: acetic acid concentration | 3–5% |
| Hypertension definition | BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg on 2 occasions |
| Diabetes: FPG diagnostic threshold | ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) confirmed on 2 occasions |
| Diabetes: HbA1c diagnostic threshold | ≥ 6.5% |
| NCD deaths as % of all global deaths | 71% (four main NCDs) |
| COTPA enacted | 2003 |
| FSSAI established under | Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 |
| IMR formula denominator | Live births |
| Secondary attack rate denominator | Susceptible household contacts |
| Sensitivity formula | TP ÷ (TP + FN) |
| Specificity formula | TN ÷ (TN + FP) |

---

## Must-know comparisons

### Marasmus vs Kwashiorkor

| Feature | Marasmus | Kwashiorkor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weight | < 60% of median | 60–80% of median |
| Oedema | Absent | Present (bilateral pitting) |
| Appearance | Severe wasting, skin and bone, old-man face | Oedema, skin lesions, pot belly |
| Hair | Sparse, dry | Discoloured (flag sign), easily plucked |
| Liver | Fatty liver (possible) | Hepatomegaly (fatty infiltration) |
| Mood | Alert, hungry | Apathetic, anorexic |
| Cause | Calories AND protein deficit | Mainly protein deficit |

### Incidence vs Prevalence

| Feature | Incidence | Prevalence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | New cases over a time period | All existing cases at one time |
| Use | Acute diseases; risk; aetiology studies | Chronic diseases; service planning |
| Formula | New cases ÷ Population at risk × constant | All cases ÷ Total population × constant |
| Relationship | Prevalence ≈ Incidence × Duration | — |

### Sensitivity vs Specificity

| Feature | Sensitivity | Specificity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formula | TP ÷ (TP + FN) | TN ÷ (TN + FP) |
| Meaning | Correctly identifies true positives | Correctly identifies true negatives |
| Use when | Missing a case is dangerous (high-stakes disease) | False positives cause harm (unnecessary treatment) |
| High means | Few false negatives | Few false positives |

### Quarantine vs Isolation

| Feature | Quarantine | Isolation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who | Well persons exposed to a communicable disease | Persons with confirmed infectious disease |
| Duration | One incubation period | Until no longer communicable |
| Goal | Prevent exposure of others if person develops disease | Prevent spread from known cases |

### Case-Control vs Cohort Study

| Feature | Case-Control | Cohort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | Retrospective (back in time from outcome) | Prospective (forward in time from exposure) |
| Start with | Cases and controls | Exposed and unexposed groups |
| Measure | Odds ratio (OR) | Relative risk (RR) |
| Good for | Rare diseases | Incidence; multiple outcomes |
| Main bias | Recall bias | Loss to follow-up |

---

## Sequences to draw from memory

### Outbreak investigation steps

```text
1. Verify diagnosis
2. Confirm it is an outbreak (numbers above baseline)
3. Define a case definition
4. Count all cases
5. Describe: person, place, time (epidemic curve)
6. Develop hypotheses
7. Test hypotheses (analytical study)
8. Implement control measures
9. Communicate findings
10. Write a report
```

### Water treatment steps

```text
Collection → Screening (remove large debris) → Sedimentation
→ Coagulation-flocculation → Sand filtration
→ Disinfection (chlorination, residual 0.2–0.5 mg/L at consumer end)
→ Storage and distribution
```

### Bag technique (home visit)

```text
On entering home:
1. Lay clean paper on a surface (clean zone).
2. Place bag on clean paper.
3. Wash hands (alcohol gel or soap and water).
4. Take out only needed items.
5. Perform procedure.
6. Place used items in a separate waste bag (dirty zone).
7. Wash hands again.
8. Repack bag (clean items only inside).
Never mix clean and dirty zones.
```

---

## National programme quick-reference

| Programme | Acronym | Target condition | Key activity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme | NTEP | TB | DOTS; GeneXpert; Nikshay portal; free drugs; Nikshay Poshan Yojana |
| Revised National TB Control Programme | RNTCP | TB | Former name of NTEP; replaced 2020 |
| National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme | NVBDCP | Malaria, dengue, filaria, kala-azar, JE, chikungunya | IRS, LLINs, MDA, ACT, RDT |
| National AIDS Control Programme | NACP | HIV/AIDS | Free ART; ICTC; PMTCT; targeted interventions |
| National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, CVD and Stroke | NPCDCS | NCDs | Population screening at HWC; NCD clinics; lifestyle counselling |
| National Leprosy Eradication Programme | NLEP | Leprosy | Free MDT |
| National Immunisation Programme / UIP | NIP / UIP | Vaccine-preventable diseases | National Immunisation Day; Mission Indradhanush |
| Integrated Child Development Services | ICDS | Children 0–6 y, pregnant and lactating women | Supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health education, pre-school education, referral |
| National Anaemia Control / Anaemia Mukt Bharat | AMB | Anaemia | IFA supplementation, deworming, dietary diversification |
| National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme | NIDDCP | IDD (goitre, cretinism) | Universal salt iodisation |
| Swachh Bharat Mission | SBM | Open defecation | Toilet construction; ODF certification |
| Poshan Abhiyaan | — | Stunting, underweight, anaemia | Multi-ministry convergence; targets stunting, wasting, anaemia, low birth weight |
| National Deworming Day | NDD | Soil-transmitted helminths | Albendazole 400 mg, 1–19 years, twice yearly |

---

## Immunisation schedule — key vaccines at a glance

| Age | Key vaccines |
| --- | --- |
| Birth | BCG, OPV₀, Hep B (birth dose) |
| 6 weeks | OPV₁, Penta₁, fIPV₁, Rotavirus₁, PCV₁ |
| 9–12 months | MR₁, JE₁ (endemic states), Vitamin A₁ |
| 16–24 months | DPT Booster₁, OPV Booster, MR₂ |
| 10 years | Td |

**Cold chain key facts**: most vaccines stored at 2–8°C; OPV at −15 to −25°C; never refreeze thawed vaccines; residual chlorine and potency testing at immunisation session.

---

## Exam reminder

- Section A (20 marks): one mark per question — use the elimination method; know acronyms (NTEP, NVBDCP, NACP, NPCDCS, ICDS); know standard rates and formulas.
- Section B (20 marks): write 2 of 3 essays; use the standard 5-part structure for any communicable disease (agent, transmission, features, diagnosis, management); always end with nursing care and community role.
- Section C (35 marks): 7 of 9 short answers; choose what you know most; for a 5-mark answer use 5 clear points; epidemiology formulas with examples and national programmes with key activities are reliable short-answer topics.
- For any community programme question: name the programme, year launched or key regulation, target group, key intervention, and implementing agency.
- For any epidemiology question involving a formula: state the formula explicitly before substituting values; write the numerator and denominator.

# Unit 1: Concepts of community health, levels of prevention, health care planning and the delivery system in India

This unit builds the base for the whole subject. It joins the INC syllabus Unit I (concepts of community health and community health nursing) and Unit II (health care planning and the delivery system) because both describe the "big picture" a community nurse works inside: what health is, how disease develops, how prevention works, and how the country is organised to deliver care.

## 1.1 Public health, community health and community health nursing

- **Public health** is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts of society. It works on whole populations, not one patient at a time.
- **Community health** is the health status of a defined group of people and the actions taken to protect and improve it. A community can be a village, an urban ward, a tribal block or a group sharing a common feature.
- **Community health nursing** is a field of nursing that blends nursing practice with public health. The family and community are the unit of service. The nurse promotes and protects health, prevents disease, and gives care at home, at health centres and in field areas, working with people rather than only for them.

**Scope of community health nursing:** health promotion and health education; maternal and child health; family planning; immunisation; nutrition; control of communicable and non-communicable diseases; school health; occupational health; care of the elderly, the disabled and the dying; environmental sanitation; and participation in national health programmes.

## 1.2 Evolution of public health in India

Public health in India grew in clear steps:

- Early sanitary work under colonial rule (sanitary commissions, control of plague and cholera outbreaks).
- The **Bhore Committee (1946)** — the Health Survey and Development Committee — gave the blueprint for a three-tier rural health service, the primary health centre idea and an "integrated" preventive-and-curative approach. Its recommendations still shape the system.
- After independence, a series of committees (see 1.7) refined the plan.
- The launch of the **National Health Mission** and, more recently, **Ayushman Bharat** with Health and Wellness Centres marks the shift towards comprehensive primary health care.

## 1.3 Concepts of health and disease

**Health** (WHO definition): a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. Later thinking adds spiritual and other dimensions and sees health as a resource for daily living, not a goal in itself.

**Dimensions of health:**

| Dimension | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Physical | Body works well; organs and systems are in order |
| Mental | Able to think clearly, cope with stress, feel balanced |
| Social | Good relationships, able to take part in society |
| Spiritual | Sense of purpose, values, meaning |
| Others | Emotional, vocational, and (for a population) environmental well-being |

Health is not a fixed point. People move along a **wellness–illness continuum**, from best possible health through reduced health to serious illness and death. The nurse's aim is to move the person and family towards the wellness end.

**Determinants of health** — the factors that decide how healthy a person or group is:

- **Biological** — age, sex, genetics.
- **Behavioural / lifestyle** — diet, physical activity, tobacco, alcohol, hygiene.
- **Environmental** — safe water, clean air, housing, sanitation, workplace.
- **Socio-economic** — income, education, occupation, food security.
- **Health services** — how available, reachable and acceptable the care is.
- **Other** — gender, culture, social support, and the wider "social determinants" such as poverty and discrimination.

## 1.4 Natural history of disease

This is the full course a disease runs in a person if nothing is done. It has two phases.

```text
   PRE-PATHOGENESIS                 PATHOGENESIS
   (before the person is ill)       (disease is present in the body)
   Agent + Host + Environment  -->  Entry/stimulus --> Early changes
   interact (the "triad")           --> Clinical disease --> Outcome
                                          (recovery / disability / death)
```

- **Pre-pathogenesis phase:** the person is still healthy, but the agent, host and environment are interacting. This is where health promotion and specific protection act.
- **Pathogenesis phase:** the agent has entered or acted on the host; tissue changes begin, signs and symptoms appear, and the disease moves to its outcome.

Knowing the natural history tells the nurse **where** to intervene — the earlier, the better.

## 1.5 Levels of prevention

Prevention is matched to the phase of disease (Leavell and Clark's model).

| Level | When it acts | What the nurse does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primordial** | Before risk factors appear | Stop risk factors from developing — healthy habits in childhood, policy for clean environment |
| **Primary** | Pre-pathogenesis | Health promotion (education, nutrition, lifestyle) and specific protection (immunisation, safe water, use of mosquito nets) |
| **Secondary** | Early pathogenesis | Early diagnosis and prompt treatment — screening camps, finding cases early |
| **Tertiary** | Late disease | Disability limitation and rehabilitation — prevent complications, restore function |

A single disease shows all levels. For diabetes: healthy diet and activity (primary), blood-sugar screening (secondary), foot care and physiotherapy after complications (tertiary).

## 1.6 Health problems (profile) of India

India faces a **double burden of disease**. The nurse should be able to name the main groups:

- **Communicable diseases** — tuberculosis, vector-borne diseases (malaria, dengue), diarrhoeal diseases, respiratory infections, HIV/AIDS, viral hepatitis.
- **Non-communicable diseases (NCDs)** — rising fast: diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, cancers, chronic lung disease, mental illness.
- **Maternal and child health problems** — anaemia, under-nutrition, maternal and newborn deaths.
- **Nutritional problems** — under-nutrition in children, anaemia, and now obesity.
- **Environmental problems** — unsafe water, poor sanitation, air pollution.
- **Demographic change** — a large young population and a growing elderly population.

Exact rates (IMR, MMR, under-five mortality) change every year; look up the **latest Sample Registration System (SRS)** and **National Family Health Survey (NFHS)** figures rather than memorising old numbers.

## 1.7 Health planning and its steps

**Health planning** is the orderly process of deciding health goals and the best way to reach them with the resources available.

Steps of health planning (a simple cycle):

1. Analysis of the health situation (assess needs and problems).
2. Setting priorities among problems.
3. Setting objectives and targets.
4. Assessing resources and constraints.
5. Choosing the best strategy / plan of action.
6. Putting the plan into action (implementation).
7. Monitoring and evaluation, then feeding results back into the next cycle.

**Community participation** is central: people and local stakeholders (panchayats, self-help groups, village health committees) help identify problems and run the plan, which makes it more acceptable and lasting.

### Committees and commissions on health (know the main ones)

| Committee / plan | Main contribution |
| --- | --- |
| Bhore Committee (1946) | Three-tier rural health service; primary health centre concept |
| Mudaliar Committee (1962) | Strengthen district hospitals; improve the quality of PHCs |
| Chadha Committee (1963) | Linked malaria and family planning work; basic health workers |
| Mukherjee Committee (1965) | Separate staff for family planning and health programmes |
| Kartar Singh Committee (1973) | Multipurpose health worker (male and female) scheme |
| Srivastava Committee (1975) | Community health workers; led to the "health for all" direction |
| Five Year Plans | The country's main tool for funding and expanding health services over successive planning periods |

## 1.8 Health care delivery system in India

The system is built in levels, from the village up to the nation, so that care gets steadily more specialised as the patient is referred upward.

```text
              NATIONAL LEVEL  (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, policy)
                     |
              STATE LEVEL     (State health department, directorates)
                     |
              DISTRICT LEVEL  (District Hospital, CMO, district programmes)
                     |
       -----------------------------------------
       |                  |                     |
   CHC (block)        PHC (cluster of           SC / HWC (nearest
   First Referral     villages)                 to the people)
   Unit, specialists  Medical officer, first    ANM/MLHP, first contact
                      referral and supervision  care, home visits
                     |
              COMMUNITY: ASHA, Anganwadi worker, family
```

**Sub-Centre (SC):** the most peripheral contact point; staffed by the ANM (and a male health worker). It gives maternal-child health, family planning, immunisation and basic care.

**Primary Health Centre (PHC):** a referral unit for sub-centres; has a medical officer and staff; provides curative and preventive care and supervises field work.

**Community Health Centre (CHC):** a block-level First Referral Unit (FRU) with specialists (medicine, surgery, obstetrics, paediatrics) and beds.

**District, State and National levels** provide more specialised hospitals, programme management, policy and funding.

> Population norms (per the Indian Public Health Standards) have long been used as roughly **one SC per 5,000 people (3,000 in hilly/tribal areas), one PHC per 30,000 (20,000 hilly/tribal), one CHC per about 80,000–1,20,000.** These norms are revised from time to time, so quote the current IPHS figure in an exam and say you would confirm it.

## 1.9 Primary health care, CPHC and the health and wellness centre

- **Primary health care (PHC as a concept)** was defined at the **Alma-Ata Declaration (1978)**, with the goal of **"Health for All"**. It means essential health care, made universally accessible, at a cost the community and country can afford, with full community participation.
- **Four principles:** equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination, and appropriate technology.
- **Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC)** widens this to cover the whole range of services across the lifespan — not just mother-and-child care but also NCDs, mental health, elderly care, palliative care and more.
- Under **Ayushman Bharat**, sub-centres and some PHCs are being upgraded to **Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs/Ayushman Arogya Mandir)** to deliver CPHC close to home. A **Mid-Level Health Provider (MLHP) / Community Health Provider (CHP)** leads the HWC team and provides an expanded package of services and screening.

## 1.10 National health policies and programmes (overview)

- **National Health Policy (1983, 2002, 2017):** successive statements of the country's health goals. The 1983 policy aimed for "Health for All"; the 2017 policy stresses universal access, reducing out-of-pocket spending and strengthening primary care.
- **National Health Mission (NHM):** the umbrella programme that combines the **National Rural Health Mission (NRHM, launched 2005)** and the **National Urban Health Mission (NUHM, launched 2013)**. It strengthens health systems, the ASHA scheme, maternal-child health and disease programmes.
- **Ayushman Bharat (2018):** has two parts — (1) **Health and Wellness Centres** for comprehensive primary care, and (2) **PM-JAY (Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana)**, a health-insurance scheme that gives eligible families cover of up to ₹5 lakh per family per year for hospital care.
- **Universal Health Coverage (UHC):** the goal that all people get the health services they need, of good quality, without financial hardship. SDG target 3.8.
- **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):** 17 global goals adopted in 2015, to be reached by 2030; **SDG 3 ("Good health and well-being")** is the main health goal, with targets on maternal and child deaths, communicable and non-communicable diseases and UHC.

(Programme details are covered again in Units 7 and 8, where each disease and its national programme are explained.)

## Remember

- Community health nursing = nursing + public health; the **family and community** are the unit of service.
- WHO health = complete physical, mental and social well-being; dimensions also include spiritual.
- Determinants: biological, behavioural, environmental, socio-economic, health services.
- Natural history: **pre-pathogenesis** (promotion, protection) → **pathogenesis** (early diagnosis, then rehabilitation).
- Prevention levels: **primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary** — match them to the disease phase.
- Delivery tiers: **SC/HWC → PHC → CHC (FRU) → District → State → National.**
- PHC concept = **Alma-Ata 1978, "Health for All"**, four principles; **CPHC** through **HWCs** led by the MLHP/CHP.
- Policies/programmes: **NHP 1983/2002/2017; NHM (NRHM 2005, NUHM 2013); Ayushman Bharat 2018 (HWC + PM-JAY); SDGs 2015, goal 3.**
- Quote current IMR/MMR and IPHS norms from the **latest SRS/NFHS and IPHS** rather than old figures.

# Unit 2: Environmental science, environmental health and sanitation

The environment is everything outside the human body that can affect health. Community health nurses work at the intersection of people and their environments — assessing hazards, educating communities, and advocating for sanitation and clean water.

---

## 2.1 Concepts of environmental health

**Environmental health** is the branch of public health concerned with all aspects of the natural and built environment that may affect human health, including physical, chemical, biological, and social factors.

**Ecology** is the study of relationships between organisms and their environment. Humans depend on healthy ecosystems for food, water, air, and climate regulation. Environmental degradation harms health directly (pollutants cause disease) and indirectly (climate change shifts disease vectors).

**Components of the environment**:
- **Physical**: climate, temperature, radiation, noise.
- **Chemical**: air pollutants, pesticides, heavy metals, industrial chemicals, water contaminants.
- **Biological**: bacteria, viruses, parasites, insects, rodents.
- **Social**: poverty, housing, education, occupation, cultural practices.

---

## 2.2 Air pollution

**Air pollutants** are substances released into the atmosphere in concentrations that are harmful.

| Pollutant | Main sources | Health effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Particulate matter (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀) | Motor vehicles, industries, construction, biomass burning | Respiratory disease (asthma, COPD), cardiovascular disease, lung cancer |
| Carbon monoxide (CO) | Incomplete combustion (vehicles, stoves) | Binds haemoglobin (COHb) → reduces O₂ carrying capacity; headache, confusion, death at high levels |
| Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) | Burning sulphur-containing fuels (coal, diesel) | Bronchoconstriction; acid rain |
| Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) | Vehicle exhaust, power plants | Respiratory irritant; photochemical smog |
| Ozone (O₃) | Photochemical reaction of NOₓ + VOCs in sunlight | Lung tissue damage; worsens asthma |
| Lead | Old paint, leaded petrol, battery industries | Neurotoxic (especially children — IQ, learning); anaemia, kidney damage |
| Indoor smoke | Burning biomass (wood, dung, crop residues) in poorly ventilated kitchens | Highest burden in India; ALRI in children, COPD in women |

**Prevention**: vehicle emission standards; catalytic converters; cleaner cooking fuels (LPG, solar cookers — Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana); industrial emission limits; urban tree cover; air quality monitoring.

**Nurse's role**: assess breathing in community surveys; identify households using solid fuels; promote ventilated stoves and clean cooking; recognise occupational exposure (painters, battery workers, miners).

---

## 2.3 Water pollution and safe water supply

Water is an essential resource and a major vehicle for disease transmission.

### Sources of drinking water

| Source | Characteristics | Safety concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rainwater (harvested) | Generally safe if collected from clean surfaces | Contamination from roof; storage vessel hygiene |
| Surface water (rivers, lakes) | Easily contaminated by sewage, agricultural runoff | Needs treatment before use |
| Groundwater (wells, boreholes) | Usually safer but can be contaminated by agricultural chemicals, natural arsenic/fluoride | Arsenic (Bangladesh/Bengal), fluoride (fluorosis in India) |
| Piped municipal supply | Treated and chlorinated | Contamination at distribution point; intermittent supply means back-siphonage |
| Hand pump (tube well) | Common in rural India | Arsenic in hand-pump water in some states |

### Water quality parameters

| Parameter | Standard (India BIS 10500) | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pH | 6.5–8.5 | Corrosion of pipes; bactericidal effect of chlorine reduced at high pH |
| Turbidity | ≤ 1 NTU (desirable), ≤ 5 NTU (acceptable) | Sediment indicates contamination; reduces chlorine efficacy |
| Total dissolved solids | ≤ 500 mg/L (desirable) | Taste; mineral content |
| Nitrate | ≤ 45 mg/L | Methaemoglobinaemia in infants (blue baby syndrome) |
| Arsenic | ≤ 0.01 mg/L | Skin cancer, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease |
| Fluoride | 0.6–1.5 mg/L (desirable) | Below 0.6: dental caries; above 1.5: dental fluorosis; above 4.0: skeletal fluorosis |
| Faecal coliforms (E. coli) | 0 per 100 mL (drinking water) | Key indicator of faecal contamination |
| Residual chlorine | 0.2–0.5 mg/L at consumer end | Disinfection maintained in distribution |

### Water treatment

```text
Collection → Screening (remove large debris) → Sedimentation → Coagulation-flocculation
  → Sand filtration → Disinfection (chlorination) → Storage and distribution
```

**Disinfection**: chlorine is the most widely used. **Boiling** kills all pathogens (reliable at household level). **Chlorination**: bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) commonly used in India; residual chlorine must be maintained. SODIS (Solar Disinfection): filling a clear PET bottle with water and exposing to sunlight for 6+ hours; practical in areas without electricity.

**Point-of-use water treatment**: boiling, chlorine tablets, ceramic filter, UV pen — teach households to use these when water quality is in doubt.

---

## 2.4 Soil pollution and solid waste management

**Soil pollutants**: agricultural chemicals (pesticides, fertilisers), heavy metals (lead, cadmium), industrial waste, domestic solid waste. Health impacts: contamination of food crops; drinking water contamination; skin absorption; inhalation of dust.

**Solid waste management (SWM)** — the 3 Rs:
- **Reduce**: buy less, avoid single-use plastics, reduce packaging.
- **Reuse**: repair and use again.
- **Recycle**: process into new material.

**Waste categories** (Solid Waste Management Rules 2016):
- **Biodegradable (wet waste)**: kitchen scraps, garden waste — composting.
- **Recyclable (dry waste)**: paper, glass, metal, plastic — segregate at source.
- **Hazardous waste**: batteries, paints, chemicals — special disposal.
- **Biomedical waste**: health facility waste — governed by BMW Management Rules 2016.

**Biomedical waste management (INC-relevant)**:
- Yellow bag: pathological, anatomical, soiled linen → incineration.
- Red bag/container: contaminated sharps, plastic, IV tubing → autoclave → shredder → landfill.
- Blue/white container: glass waste → autoclave → landfill.
- Black bag: general waste.
- Never mix biomedical waste with general waste.

---

## 2.5 Environmental sanitation

**Sanitation** covers excreta disposal, wastewater disposal, solid waste management, control of insects and rodents, food hygiene, and housing conditions.

### Excreta disposal

**Sanitary latrine**: a facility that prevents excreta from contaminating water, soil and food, and prevents access by insects and rodents. The ideal latrine is:
- Watertight pit or septic tank.
- Fly-proof cover slab.
- Superstructure for privacy.
- Water seal (pit latrine/pour-flush latrine).

**Types of latrines in India**: pit latrine, bore-hole latrine, dug well latrine, aquaprivy, septic tank + soak pit (most effective), sewerage system (urban ideal).

**Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)**: the Government of India's programme to end open defecation. By 2019, over 100 million toilets were constructed; rural areas declared Open Defecation Free (ODF).

**Faecal-oral route diseases**: typhoid, cholera, hepatitis A, polio, amoebiasis, giardiasis — all prevented by sanitary excreta disposal + safe water + hand hygiene.

### Housing and health

**A healthy house** provides:
- Protection from the elements (rain, cold, heat).
- Personal space (overcrowding spreads airborne diseases — TB, measles).
- Ventilation (removes indoor air pollutants and reduces humidity).
- Safe water supply and sanitation.
- Refuse disposal.
- Lighting — natural and artificial.
- Safe electrical installation.
- Absence of dampness (mould → respiratory disease).

**Overcrowding** is defined as more than 2 persons per sleeping room (WHO). Overcrowding increases transmission of respiratory and skin infections.

---

## 2.6 Vector control

**Vectors** are organisms that transmit pathogens from one host to another.

| Vector | Disease | Control measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Anopheles* mosquito | Malaria | Eliminate breeding sites (stagnant water), insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs), indoor residual spraying (IRS), larviciding (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, temephos), adult mosquito control, anti-larval fish (*Gambusia*) |
| *Aedes aegypti* | Dengue, Zika, chikungunya | Same as above; emphasise removal of artificial containers with water (tyres, flower pots, overhead tanks) |
| *Culex* mosquito | Lymphatic filariasis (Bancroftian), Japanese encephalitis | Drain rice fields; larvicide; IRS; bed nets |
| Housefly | Typhoid, cholera, dysentery, amoebiasis | Cover food; dispose refuse; cover latrines; proper sewage; sanitary food handling |
| Cockroach | Typhoid, dysentery | Good kitchen hygiene; insecticides in crevices |
| Rat/flea | Plague, leptospirosis | Rat-proofing buildings; trapping; rodenticides; flea control |
| Sandfly | Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) | IRS with DDT (India); avoid sandfly bites |

**Integrated vector management (IVM)**: a rational, evidence-based approach combining several control methods (biological, chemical, environmental, personal protection) to maximise effect and minimise harm.

---

## 2.7 Occupational health and environmental hazards

**Occupational health** (nurses' role in the community):
- Assess workplace hazards during home visits or community surveys.
- Identify occupation-related diseases (silicosis, asbestosis, NIHL, occupational asthma).
- Refer to Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) for workers' health care.
- Advise on personal protective equipment.

**Climate change and health**:
- Increasing temperatures expand the range of *Anopheles* (malaria) and *Aedes* (dengue) mosquitoes.
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts) damage water and sanitation infrastructure.
- Food insecurity increases with unpredictable rainfall.
- Heat stress is a direct health risk for outdoor workers and older adults.

**Nurse's advocacy role**: participate in local health committees; report environmental hazards to the panchayat or municipal health officer; educate communities about pollution-linked disease; support SBM and clean cooking programmes.

# Unit 3: Nutrition assessment and education, food borne diseases and food safety

Malnutrition in India affects both extremes — undernutrition (stunting, wasting, anaemia) and overnutrition (obesity, non-communicable diseases). The community health nurse plays a central role in assessing nutritional status, delivering food and nutrition education, and ensuring food safety.

---

## 3.1 Nutrition concepts

**Nutrition** is the process by which the body takes in and uses food for growth, repair and maintenance. **Malnutrition** includes both undernutrition and overnutrition.

**Nutrients and their roles**:

| Nutrient | Key sources | Functions | Deficiency disease |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates | Rice, wheat, sugar, potato | Main energy source (4 kcal/g) | — |
| Proteins | Pulses, legumes, meat, egg, milk, soy | Growth, repair, enzymes, antibodies | Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency), Marasmus (calorie deficiency) |
| Fats | Oils, nuts, dairy, meat | Energy (9 kcal/g), fat-soluble vitamins, cell membranes | Essential fatty acid deficiency |
| Vitamin A | Liver, egg, dairy, dark-green vegetables, orange/yellow fruits | Vision (rhodopsin), immunity, epithelial integrity | Night blindness, xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots |
| Vitamin D | Sunlight (skin synthesis), fish liver oil, fortified foods | Calcium absorption, bone mineralisation | Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults) |
| Vitamin B₁₂ | Animal foods only (meat, fish, dairy, eggs) | Myelin synthesis, DNA synthesis | Megaloblastic anaemia, subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord |
| Folate | Green leafy vegetables, legumes, fortified grain | DNA synthesis (esp. neural tube formation) | Megaloblastic anaemia; neural tube defects (NTDs) in pregnancy |
| Vitamin C | Citrus fruits, tomatoes, amla | Collagen synthesis, immunity, iron absorption | Scurvy (perifollicular petechiae, bleeding gums, wound healing failure) |
| Iron | Meat (haem iron), legumes, green leafy vegetables (non-haem iron) | Haemoglobin, myoglobin, enzymes | Iron-deficiency anaemia (most common nutritional problem in India) |
| Iodine | Iodised salt, seafood | Thyroid hormone synthesis | Goitre, hypothyroidism, cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism) |
| Calcium | Dairy, green leafy vegetables, sesame | Bone, teeth, muscle contraction, coagulation | Osteoporosis, rickets |
| Zinc | Meat, legumes, nuts | Growth, immunity, wound healing, taste | Growth retardation, immune suppression, diarrhoea |

---

## 3.2 Nutritional assessment

**ABCD method** of nutritional assessment:

| Component | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| **A — Anthropometric** | Weight, height, BMI, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), skin fold thickness, head circumference (children), waist:hip ratio |
| **B — Biochemical** | Haemoglobin, serum albumin/prealbumin, serum retinol (Vitamin A), TSH/T4 (iodine), urine iodine concentration |
| **C — Clinical** | Physical signs of deficiency (Bitot's spots, pallor, oedema, skin changes, hair changes, angular stomatitis, glossitis, goitre) |
| **D — Dietary** | 24-hour dietary recall, food frequency questionnaire, dietary diversity score |

### Anthropometric indices for children (WHO standards)

| Index | Measure | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weight-for-age (W/A) | Underweight | Below −2 SD = underweight; below −3 SD = severe underweight; global malnutrition indicator |
| Height-for-age (H/A) | Stunting | Below −2 SD = stunted (chronic undernutrition / past malnutrition) |
| Weight-for-height (W/H) | Wasting | Below −2 SD = wasted (acute undernutrition / current crisis) |
| MUAC | Acute malnutrition | < 11.5 cm = severe acute malnutrition (SAM); 11.5–12.5 cm = MAM |

**Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)** can be measured with a simple tape; it is used at community level for screening without weighing or measuring height. < 23 cm in pregnant women indicates acute malnutrition.

### Classification of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) in children

| Grade | W/A (% of median) | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marasmus | < 60% | Severe wasting, muscle loss, old-man face, skin and bone; NO oedema; hungry, alert |
| Kwashiorkor | 60–80% | Oedema (pitting, bilateral), skin lesions, hair discolouration and thinning (flag sign), liver enlargement; anorexia, apathetic |
| Marasmic-kwashiorkor | < 60% with oedema | Both features; most severely ill |

**Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)** management:
- Phase 1 (stabilisation, 2 weeks): treat infection, correct metabolic complications, cautious re-feeding (F-75 formula, 100 kcal/kg/day).
- Phase 2 (rehabilitation): high-energy formula (F-100, RUTF — Ready to Use Therapeutic Food), catch-up growth.
- Avoid high sodium; risk of re-feeding syndrome (hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia).

---

## 3.3 Nutritional programmes in India

| Programme | Target group | Key intervention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) | Children 0–6 years, pregnant and lactating mothers | Supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, health check-up, immunisation, nutrition counselling, referral services |
| Mid-Day Meal Scheme (MDMS) | School children (Classes I–VIII) | Cooked meal at school; reduces hunger and improves attendance |
| Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN) | School children | Renamed from MDMS; focus on nutritional quality and fortification |
| National Anaemia Control Programme / Anaemia Mukt Bharat | Women, children, adolescents | Iron and folic acid supplementation; deworming; dietary diversification |
| National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP) | All population | Universal iodisation of salt; monitoring of iodine levels |
| Vitamin A Supplementation Programme | Children 6 months–5 years | High-dose Vitamin A every 6 months; integrated with immunisation rounds |
| Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) | Pregnant and lactating women | Cash transfer of ₹5,000 for first living child to incentivise early ANC and exclusive breastfeeding |
| Poshan Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission) | Women and children | Multi-ministry convergence; targets to reduce stunting, underweight, anaemia, and low birth weight |

---

## 3.4 Nutrition during special life stages

**Infant feeding**:
- Initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth (colostrum — immunoglobulins, lactoferrin, oligosaccharides).
- **Exclusive breastfeeding** for 6 months (no water, juice, or other foods).
- Complementary feeding from 6 months: soft, nutrient-dense foods; continue breastfeeding up to 2 years.
- Breastfeeding benefits: reduces GI infections, ALRI, SIDS; promotes cognitive development; reduces maternal risk of ovarian and breast cancer.

**Adolescent nutrition**: iron and folate for girls (menstrual losses); calcium for bone density; avoid early marriage (adolescent pregnancy → higher maternal and infant mortality); address eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia — common in girls).

**Pregnancy**: additional 300 kcal/day in 2nd and 3rd trimester; iron and folic acid from first trimester (400 µg folic acid before conception reduces NTD risk); calcium supplementation; avoid alcohol, tobacco.

**Lactation**: additional 500 kcal/day; increased water, protein, calcium, iodine, and vitamin D needs.

**Older adults**: reduced caloric need but maintained need for protein, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin B₁₂; risk of undernutrition, dehydration, and drug-nutrient interactions.

---

## 3.5 Food-borne diseases

**Food-borne disease (foodborne illness)** results from consuming contaminated food. Sources of contamination: bacteria, viruses, parasites, chemicals, natural toxins.

### Major food-borne infections

| Disease | Organism | Source | Symptoms | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Typhoid | *Salmonella typhi* | Contaminated water/food (sewage-contaminated) | Stepped fever (rose spots, relative bradycardia), GI symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly; complications: intestinal perforation | Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin; ceftriaxone for severe |
| Cholera | *Vibrio cholerae* | Contaminated water and food | Rice-water diarrhoea, severe dehydration; vomiting; rapid fluid loss | ORS (or IV fluids); doxycycline or azithromycin (shortens illness) |
| Hepatitis A | Hepatitis A virus (HAV) | Faecal-oral route; contaminated water, shellfish | Jaundice, fever, anorexia, malaise; self-limiting | Supportive; HAV vaccine available |
| Staphylococcal food poisoning | *S. aureus* toxin (pre-formed) | Contaminated food left at room temperature (cream cakes, custard) | Sudden onset vomiting and diarrhoea within 2–6 hours; NO fever | Supportive; self-limiting; antibiotics not needed (toxin-mediated) |
| Salmonellosis | *Salmonella* spp. (non-typhoidal) | Poultry, eggs, meat | Diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal cramp, fever; 12–72 hours incubation | Rehydration; antibiotics only for severe or immunocompromised |
| *E. coli* diarrhoea | ETEC, EHEC, etc. | Contaminated water, undercooked meat, raw vegetables | ETEC: watery diarrhoea (traveller's diarrhoea); EHEC (O157:H7): bloody diarrhoea, haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) | Rehydration; avoid antibiotics in EHEC (risk of HUS) |
| Botulism | *Clostridium botulinum* toxin | Home-canned or preserved foods | Descending flaccid paralysis starting from cranial nerves (diplopia, dysphagia), no fever, constipation | Antitoxin (trivalent); ventilatory support; intensive care |
| Brucellosis | *Brucella* spp. | Unpasteurised milk/dairy products, contact with infected animals | Undulant fever, joint pain, hepatosplenomegaly; chronic fatigue | Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks |

---

## 3.6 Food safety

**Food safety** involves practices to prevent food-borne illness across the food chain (production, processing, storage, distribution, preparation, consumption).

**Key food safety practices**:
- **Clean**: wash hands before cooking and eating; wash fruits and vegetables with clean water.
- **Separate**: raw meat, poultry and seafood away from ready-to-eat food; separate cutting boards.
- **Cook**: cook food to safe internal temperature (meat: 75°C core temperature); no pink pork or poultry.
- **Chill**: refrigerate perishables within 2 hours; keep cold foods below 5°C; hot foods above 60°C.
- **Do not eat**: foods past expiry date; unlabelled or bulging cans; suspicious street food.

**Food adulteration**: deliberate addition of inferior or harmful substances. Examples: milk adulteration with water or urea; ghee with animal fat; spices with sawdust or colour; pulses with Kesari dal (lathyrism risk).

**Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) 1954** and **Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA) 2006**: legal framework for food quality in India. The **Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)** regulates food safety standards, licensing, and testing.

**Nurse's role in food safety**: food hygiene counselling in antenatal and child health clinics; identify food adulteration or contamination hazards in community surveys; report to local health officers; support community kitchen gardens (nutritional security) and homestead food production.

# Unit 4: Behaviour change communication, health education, and community health nursing approaches

Health behaviour change is at the heart of community health nursing. This unit covers the science and practice of health education, BCC strategies, theories of behaviour change, and the approaches community health nurses use to work with individuals, families, and communities.

---

## 4.1 Health education

**Health education** is the process of helping people acquire knowledge, attitudes, and practices that promote and protect health. It differs from health information, which is one-way communication; health education is interactive and aims for behaviour change.

**Goals of health education**:
1. Enable people to make informed choices about health.
2. Modify unhealthy behaviours (smoking, alcohol, poor diet, unsafe sex).
3. Promote healthy behaviours (vaccination, breastfeeding, hand hygiene, safe sanitation).
4. Develop life skills (communication, decision making, refusal skills).
5. Empower communities to address their own health problems.

**Principles of health education**:
- Start from where people are (knowledge, attitudes, practices).
- Use simple, local language; avoid medical jargon.
- Base content on felt needs of the community.
- Involve participants actively (not lecture alone).
- Repeat key messages consistently.
- Use multiple methods and channels.
- Evaluate whether behaviour change has occurred.

---

## 4.2 Behaviour Change Communication (BCC)

**BCC** is a systematic, evidence-based approach to changing health behaviours and social norms through communication strategies tailored to specific audiences.

**BCC vs IEC**:
- **IEC** (Information, Education, Communication): traditional approach; provides information and educates — often one-way.
- **BCC**: builds on IEC; emphasises social and behavioural factors; uses participatory methods; targets specific barriers to change.

**Key elements of effective BCC**:
- **Audience analysis**: understand the target audience's knowledge, attitudes, practices, barriers, and motivators before designing messages.
- **Message design**: clear, simple, action-oriented messages (not "eat nutritious food" but "eat one palm-sized portion of dal every day").
- **Channel selection**: appropriate media for the audience (community meeting, radio, mobile SMS, street play, women's self-help group).
- **Pretesting**: test materials on a sample of the target audience before wide distribution.
- **Feedback and evaluation**: measure whether behaviour changed, not just knowledge.

---

## 4.3 Theories and models of behaviour change

### Health Belief Model (HBM)

Developed in the 1950s to explain why people do not use preventive health services. A person will take a health action if they believe:
1. **Perceived susceptibility**: "I can get this disease."
2. **Perceived severity**: "This disease is serious."
3. **Perceived benefits**: "This action will protect me."
4. **Perceived barriers**: "The barriers to action are manageable."
5. **Cues to action**: a trigger event (symptom, reminder, media message) prompts action.
6. **Self-efficacy**: "I am able to do this."

**Application**: designing messages that increase perceived susceptibility (risk communication) and reduce perceived barriers (address cost, access, side effects of vaccines).

### Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Change)

Developed by Prochaska and DiClemente. Behaviour change is a process, not a single event. People move through stages:

| Stage | Description | Communication strategy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-contemplation | Not thinking about change; not aware of the problem | Raise awareness; personalise risk |
| Contemplation | Aware; thinking about change; ambivalent | Explore pros and cons; motivational interviewing |
| Preparation | Intending to change soon; planning | Help make a concrete plan; build confidence |
| Action | Actively making behaviour change | Support; encourage; reinforce |
| Maintenance | Sustaining the change for > 6 months | Prevent relapse; build social support |
| Relapse | Returns to old behaviour | Normalise; encourage to try again; analyse triggers |

### Social Cognitive Theory (Bandura)

**Self-efficacy** (confidence to perform a behaviour) is the key predictor of behaviour change. Learning occurs through **observation** (watching others succeed) and **modelling** (seeing someone like yourself do it). Use peer educators, community champions, and role-play demonstrations.

### PRECEDE-PROCEED model

A community diagnosis framework:
- **PRECEDE** (planning): identify the health problem, its behavioural and environmental determinants, and the predisposing/enabling/reinforcing factors.
- **PROCEED** (implementation and evaluation): implement the programme and evaluate at multiple levels.

**Predisposing factors**: knowledge, attitudes, beliefs, values, perceptions.
**Enabling factors**: availability, accessibility, affordability of health services; skills.
**Reinforcing factors**: social support, peer norms, media, family influence.

---

## 4.4 Communication methods and media

### Individual communication
- **Counselling**: one-to-one interaction; most effective for sensitive issues (HIV, family planning, substance abuse).
- **Home visits**: nurse visits the family in their own home; most effective for follow-up, care of bedridden or housebound patients, and for assessing home environment.

### Group communication
- **Group discussion**: 8–15 persons; interactive; promotes shared problem solving.
- **Lecture**: 10–50 persons; efficient for information delivery; less interactive.
- **Demonstration**: showing a skill (ORS preparation, breastfeeding technique, hand hygiene); always do a return demonstration.
- **Role play**: acting out scenarios; effective for skill development and stigma reduction (e.g. HIV disclosure, negotiating condom use).
- **Street play (Nukkad Natak)**: public drama; reaches low-literacy audiences; uses entertainment-education.

### Mass communication
- **Print media**: posters, pamphlets, flip charts, newspapers; effective for literate audiences.
- **Radio**: reaches rural areas with low literacy; local language; health programmes on community radio.
- **Television and digital**: video demonstrations; social media campaigns; WhatsApp groups for health messages; effective for broader audiences.
- **Mobile phone SMS**: reminders for immunisation, ANC visits, medication adherence.

**Selection of communication channel**: consider literacy level, language, accessibility, cost, reach, feedback potential.

---

## 4.5 Community health nursing approaches

### Visiting the community

**Community health survey**: a systematic assessment of a defined community's health status, resources, and needs. Components:
- Demographic data: population, age-sex composition, vital events.
- Health status data: morbidity (disease burden), mortality rates, nutritional status.
- Environmental data: water, sanitation, housing, air pollution.
- Health services data: facilities, utilisation rates, immunisation coverage.
- Socioeconomic data: income, education, occupations.
- Community resources: women's groups, NGOs, local government.

### Home visit

A **home visit** is a professional visit by a community health nurse to a family at their residence.

**Purposes**:
- Assessment of health problems in the natural environment.
- Delivery of nursing care (wound dressing, injection, health education).
- Follow-up of communicable disease contacts.
- Maternal and child health services.
- Assessment of environmental hazards.

**Principles of a home visit**:
1. Plan the visit in advance (purpose, materials needed).
2. Identify yourself and obtain consent.
3. Respect the family's privacy and cultural practices.
4. Maintain confidentiality.
5. Keep records; report any concerns to the team.

**Bag technique**: the community health nurse's bag must be maintained clean (clean outside, clean inside technique). Lay a protective paper on a surface; take out only what is needed; wash hands before and after procedures; contaminated materials go into a separate bag for disposal or sterilisation.

### Community diagnosis

**Community diagnosis** is the process of identifying health problems and their determinants in a defined community, in order to plan and prioritise interventions.

Steps:
1. Define the community and its boundaries.
2. Collect data (survey, review of records, focus groups, key informant interviews).
3. Analyse data: identify leading causes of death, morbidity, risk factors.
4. Set priorities (severity, frequency, feasibility of intervention, community concern).
5. Plan, implement and evaluate interventions.

### Community organisation

**Community organisation** is the process of helping a community to identify its needs, develop confidence to act, find resources, and take action.

**Key principles**: participatory; community-led; builds on existing strengths; respects culture; promotes self-reliance; avoids dependency.

**Community participation levels** (Arnstein's ladder): from manipulation/therapy (lowest — token) through consultation, partnership, to citizen control (highest — genuine participation).

**Self-Help Groups (SHGs)**: in India, SHGs (especially of women) are powerful community platforms for health promotion — ASHA workers often link with SHGs to address reproductive health, nutrition, sanitation, and domestic violence.

### Epidemiological approach in community nursing

Community health nurses use epidemiological thinking to identify patterns of disease:
- **Host-Agent-Environment triad** (Epidemiological triad): all three must interact for disease to occur.
- **Levels of prevention**: primordial (address upstream determinants), primary (prevent disease before it occurs), secondary (early detection and treatment), tertiary (rehabilitation).
- **Surveillance**: ongoing collection and analysis of health data to detect trends and outbreaks; notify communicable diseases to district health authorities.

# Unit 5: Family health care, primary care in the community, records and school health services

The family is the basic unit of community health nursing care. Primary health care delivered at community level reaches populations that hospitals cannot. School health services protect children during their most formative years. This unit covers each of these areas.

---

## 5.1 Family health

**Family** is a group of individuals related by blood, marriage, adoption, or mutual interdependence. The family is the basic social unit and the fundamental unit of community health nursing care.

**Family health** encompasses the physical, mental, social, and emotional health of all family members and the functioning of the family as a unit.

### Types of families in India

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Nuclear family | Couple and their unmarried children |
| Joint (extended) family | Multiple generations or related families living together |
| Three-generation family | Grandparents, parents, and children |
| Single-parent family | One parent and children |
| Reconstituted / blended | Step-parents and step-children |

### Family health assessment

A complete family health assessment includes:
- **Family structure**: type, number, ages, relationships.
- **Family function**: communication, decision-making, roles, support systems.
- **Health status of each member**: illnesses, disabilities, immunisation status.
- **Socioeconomic factors**: income, housing, education, occupation.
- **Environmental factors**: water, sanitation, food security, hazards.
- **Health-seeking behaviour**: use of health services, traditional practices, barriers to care.

**Genogram**: a visual representation of a family structure across generations, showing health conditions and relationships. Used to identify hereditary conditions and family health patterns.

**Family risk assessment**: identify high-risk families for priority visiting — families with infants, pregnant women, elderly, disabilities, communicable disease, domestic violence, poverty.

### Family nursing process

**Assessment → Nursing Diagnosis → Planning → Implementation → Evaluation**

The community health nurse works with the family (not just the individual patient) as the client. The focus is on **family strengths** as well as problems, and on building the family's capacity to care for its members.

---

## 5.2 Reproductive and child health (RCH) in the community

Reproductive and Child Health services are the core of family health care delivered by ASHA, ANM, and community health nurses.

### Antenatal care (ANC)

**National recommendation** (National Health Mission): minimum 4 ANC visits (earlier 4, now WHO recommends 8+). Components at each visit:
- Blood pressure measurement.
- Weight and fundal height assessment.
- Urinalysis (protein, glucose).
- Haemoglobin.
- Foetal heart rate and position.
- Immunisation (TT/Td vaccination).
- Iron and folic acid supplementation.
- Counselling (diet, rest, danger signs, institutional delivery).

**Danger signs in pregnancy** (refer immediately): bleeding, severe headache with visual disturbance, swelling of face/hands/legs, reduced or absent foetal movements, prolonged labour, fever.

**Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA)**: monthly fixed-day ANC clinics at PHCs and CHCs; doctor-led examination for all pregnant women on the 9th of every month.

### Postnatal care

- Minimum 3 postnatal home visits: within 24 hours, Day 3, and Day 7 (and Day 14 and Day 42 as needed).
- Assess uterine involution, lochia, episiotomy/C-section wound, breastfeeding, immunisation (BCG, OPV₀, Hep B₀ at birth or within 24 hours), mental state (postnatal depression).
- Exclusive breastfeeding support.

### Immunisation schedule (National Immunisation Schedule 2023)

| Age | Vaccines |
| --- | --- |
| Birth | BCG, OPV₀, Hepatitis B (Birth Dose) |
| 6 weeks | OPV₁, Penta₁ (DPT+HepB+Hib), IPV₁, Rotavirus₁, PCV₁, fIPV₁ |
| 10 weeks | OPV₂, Penta₂, Rotavirus₂, PCV₂ |
| 14 weeks | OPV₃, Penta₃, IPV₂, Rotavirus₃, PCV₃ |
| 9–12 months | Measles-Rubella (MR)₁, JE₁ (endemic states), Vitamin A₁ |
| 16–24 months | DPT Booster₁, OPV Booster, MR₂, JE₂, Vitamin A₂ |
| 5–6 years | DPT Booster₂ |
| 10 years | Td |
| 16 years | Td |

**Cold chain**: vaccines must be stored at correct temperatures (most vaccines 2–8°C; OPV −15 to −25°C) throughout the supply chain. Any break in cold chain makes vaccines ineffective. The cold chain equipment includes ILR (Ice-Lined Refrigerator), deep freezers, cold boxes, vaccine carriers, and ice packs.

**Adverse Events Following Immunisation (AEFI)**: any untoward reaction after vaccination. Report to block/district health authorities. Classify as: vaccine-related, programme error, coincidental, injection-related, unknown. BCG lymphadenopathy, local redness/swelling (DPT), febrile seizure (DPT/MMR) are common mild AEFIs. Anaphylaxis is a rare severe AEFI — epinephrine must be available at all immunisation sessions.

---

## 5.3 Primary health care in India

**Primary Health Care (PHC)** as defined at Alma-Ata (1978): essential health care made universally accessible to individuals and families in the community at a cost the community and country can afford. It is the first level of contact between the community and the health system.

**Eight elements of PHC (Alma-Ata)**: education about health problems and methods of prevention and control; promotion of food supply and proper nutrition; adequate supply of safe water and basic sanitation; maternal and child health care including family planning; immunisation against major infectious diseases; prevention and control of locally endemic diseases; appropriate treatment of common diseases and injuries; provision of essential drugs.

### Rural health infrastructure (India)

| Facility | Population served | Level | Staff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sub-Centre (SC) | 3,000–5,000 | Peripheral | ANM, Male Health Worker (MPW) |
| Primary Health Centre (PHC) | 20,000–30,000 (plain) / 10,000–20,000 (hilly/tribal) | 1st level referral | Medical Officer, ANM, PHN, lab technician |
| Community Health Centre (CHC) | 80,000–1,20,000 | 2nd level referral | 4 specialists (surgery, medicine, obstetrics, paediatrics) |
| District Hospital | District | 3rd level | Multi-speciality |

**Health and Wellness Centre (HWC)**: upgraded Sub-Centres and PHCs under Ayushman Bharat (2018); deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC) including NCD screening, mental health, oral health, and palliative care; staffed by Community Health Officers (CHO) with 6-month bridge course.

**ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist)**: a community health worker, usually a woman from the same community (1 per 1,000 population in rural areas). Roles include: birth registration, immunisation mobilisation, ANC tracking, institutional delivery promotion, DOTS supporter (TB), condom and OCP distribution, linking community to health system. Paid by performance-based incentives (PBIs).

---

## 5.4 Community health records

**Health records** are a legal document and an essential tool for planning, monitoring, and evaluating health services.

### Records maintained at community level

| Record | Maintained by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Family folder / household survey register | ANM/PHN | Demographic details, health status, immunisation records of all family members in a subcentre area |
| Eligible couple register | ANM | Women aged 15–45 in reproductive union; for family planning tracking |
| Antenatal register | ANM | All registered pregnant women; ANC visits, TT, IFA, risk factors |
| Immunisation register | ANM | Child immunisation records; due-list for each session |
| MCH register | ANM | Maternal and child health events (births, deaths, ANC, PNC) |
| BPL register | ANM/ASHA | Below-poverty-line families; priority for social welfare schemes |
| Outreach session diary | ANM | Record of activities conducted at each session site |
| ASHA activity register | ASHA | Home visits, referrals, services delivered |
| Disease surveillance register | PHC | Notifiable diseases reported; feeds into IDSP |

**Integrated Health Management Portal (IHMP)** and **Mother and Child Tracking System (MCTS/RCH Portal)**: online registration of pregnant women and children to track services; generates due-lists automatically for ANMs and ASHAs.

### Reports

| Report | Frequency | Sent from → to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MPW (F) monthly report | Monthly | SC → PHC |
| MO's monthly report | Monthly | PHC → Block / BPMU |
| Form P (vital events) | Monthly | SC → PHC |
| IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme) S, P, L forms | Weekly | PHC/CHC → District → State → Centre |

---

## 5.5 School health services

**School health services** promote the health of school children (6–18 years — approximately 250 million children in India) during the most formative years of physical and mental development.

**Components of a school health programme**:
1. **Health appraisal**: annual health examination; vision, hearing, dental, growth assessment; identify and refer problems.
2. **Health promotion**: health education in curriculum (hygiene, nutrition, life skills, reproductive health for older students); physical exercise.
3. **Prevention and control of communicable diseases**: maintain immunisation records; identify contacts in outbreaks; deworming (Albendazole 400 mg twice yearly under National Deworming Day); manage outbreaks (school closure if necessary).
4. **Healthful school environment**: safe water and sanitation (Wash in Schools — WinS); clean toilets (separate for girls — a reason girls drop out); safe playground; safe food in canteen.
5. **Nutrition services**: Mid-Day Meal; monitoring for malnutrition; anaemia screening and IFA supplementation (weekly IFA for 10–19 years under WIFS — Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation programme).
6. **Mental health services**: counselling; identify children with learning disabilities, ADHD, anxiety, depression; anti-bullying programmes.
7. **School health records**: individual health cards; vision and hearing records; vaccination status; growth charts.
8. **Training school teachers**: health education, first aid, identification of health problems.

**Adolescent Reproductive and Sexual Health (ARSH) programme**: health education for 10–19-year-olds; Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) — covers nutrition, mental health, substance abuse, sexual health, injuries, non-communicable diseases for adolescents.

**National Deworming Day**: 10 February and 10 August (bi-annual); children aged 1–19 years receive Albendazole 400 mg; reduces soil-transmitted helminth burden which causes anaemia, malnutrition, and impaired learning.

**School nurse role**: annual health check; first aid; health education; case referral; liaison with parents and teachers; maintaining records; leading health days (World Health Day, No Tobacco Day).
