# Unit 6: Introduction to epidemiology — approaches, processes and investigation of an epidemic

Epidemiology is the scientific foundation of public health. It tells us who gets sick, where, when, and why — essential information for designing and evaluating community health interventions.

---

## 6.1 Definitions and scope

**Epidemiology** is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to control health problems. (Last, John M.)

**Uses of epidemiology**:
- Determine the burden of disease (frequency, distribution).
- Identify risk factors for disease (determinants).
- Evaluate the effectiveness of interventions (clinical trials, programme evaluation).
- Plan and allocate health services.
- Monitor changes in disease patterns over time (surveillance).

**Epidemiological triad**: every disease requires interaction between:
- **Host**: the person who gets the disease (age, sex, immunity, genetics, behaviour).
- **Agent**: the cause (bacteria, virus, chemical, nutrient deficiency, physical force).
- **Environment**: the conditions that facilitate transmission (water quality, temperature, vector presence, social conditions).

For disease to occur, the agent must be present in sufficient quantity, the host must be susceptible, and the environment must permit exposure.

---

## 6.2 Measures of disease frequency

### Rates

A **rate** is the frequency of a health event in a population over a specified time period.

| Measure | Formula | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crude Birth Rate | (Births ÷ Midyear population) × 1,000 | Measure of fertility |
| Crude Death Rate (CDR) | (Deaths ÷ Midyear population) × 1,000 | Overall mortality |
| Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) | (Deaths < 1 year ÷ Live births) × 1,000 | Key indicator of child health and health system performance |
| Neonatal Mortality Rate | (Deaths < 28 days ÷ Live births) × 1,000 | Early neonatal care quality |
| Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) | (Maternal deaths ÷ Live births) × 100,000 | Obstetric care quality |
| Under-5 Mortality Rate (U5MR) | (Deaths < 5 years ÷ Live births) × 1,000 | Child survival |
| Proportional Mortality Ratio | (Deaths from cause X ÷ All deaths) × 100 | Relative importance of a cause |
| Attack Rate | (New cases during outbreak ÷ Population at risk) × 100 | Used in outbreak investigation |
| Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) | (New cases among contacts ÷ Susceptible contacts) × 100 | Transmissibility of disease in households |

### Incidence vs Prevalence

| Measure | Definition | Formula | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Incidence** | New cases of a disease in a population over a specified time period | New cases ÷ Population at risk × constant | How fast is the disease occurring? |
| **Prevalence** | All existing cases (new + old) at a point in time (point prevalence) or during a period (period prevalence) | All existing cases ÷ Total population × constant | How much disease is in the population? |

**Relationship**: Prevalence ≈ Incidence × Duration of disease. A chronic disease (long duration) has high prevalence relative to incidence. A short, acute disease (brief duration) has prevalence ≈ incidence.

**Uses**: incidence is used for acute diseases and to measure risk; prevalence is used for chronic diseases and health service planning.

---

## 6.3 Study designs in epidemiology

| Study type | Description | Use | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Descriptive** (surveys, case reports, ecological) | Describe distribution of disease in terms of person, place, time | Generate hypotheses; plan interventions | Cannot prove causation |
| **Case-control** | Compare cases (with disease) to controls (without) for past exposures | Study rare diseases; test hypotheses; quick and inexpensive | Recall bias; cannot calculate incidence |
| **Cohort (prospective)** | Follow exposed and unexposed groups over time for disease development | Calculate incidence and relative risk; multiple outcomes | Expensive; long follow-up; loss to follow-up |
| **Cross-sectional** | Measure exposure and disease at the same point in time | Prevalence; screening; planning | Cannot determine temporal relationship |
| **Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT)** | Randomly allocate participants to intervention or control; gold standard | Causation; intervention efficacy | Ethical constraints; expensive; may not reflect real world |

**Relative risk (RR)**: risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; used in cohort studies. RR > 1 means increased risk; RR < 1 means protective.

**Odds ratio (OR)**: used in case-control studies; approximate RR for rare diseases. OR = (cases exposed × controls unexposed) ÷ (cases unexposed × controls exposed).

---

## 6.4 Epidemiological causation

**Association vs causation**: a statistical association between two variables does not necessarily mean one causes the other.

**Bradford Hill criteria** for causality (evidence that an association is causal):
1. Strength of association (high OR or RR).
2. Consistency (same result in different populations and settings).
3. Specificity (exposure linked to one disease).
4. Temporality (exposure precedes disease — essential criterion).
5. Biological gradient (dose-response relationship).
6. Plausibility (biologically plausible mechanism).
7. Coherence (consistent with known biology and natural history).
8. Experiment (disease decreases when exposure is removed).
9. Analogy (similar agent causes similar disease).

---

## 6.5 Screening

**Screening** is the application of a test to identify individuals at increased risk of a condition so they can be referred for further investigation and treatment.

**Criteria for a good screening programme** (Wilson and Jungner):
- The condition must be an important health problem.
- Effective treatment must be available.
- Facilities for diagnosis and treatment must be available.
- There must be a recognisable latent or early symptomatic stage.
- A suitable screening test must exist.
- The test must be acceptable to the population.
- The natural history of the condition must be understood.
- An agreed policy on who to treat must exist.
- The benefit must outweigh the harm.
- The cost must be balanced against benefits.

**Sensitivity and specificity**:

| Measure | Formula | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sensitivity | TP ÷ (TP + FN) | Ability to detect true cases; high sensitivity → few false negatives; use for serious diseases where missing a case is dangerous |
| Specificity | TN ÷ (TN + FP) | Ability to identify true non-cases; high specificity → few false positives; use when false positives cause harm (unnecessary treatment, anxiety) |
| Positive predictive value (PPV) | TP ÷ (TP + FP) | Proportion of positive tests that are true cases; depends on prevalence |
| Negative predictive value (NPV) | TN ÷ (TN + FN) | Proportion of negative tests that are true non-cases |

**India's national screening programmes**: CPHC screening for 30 conditions including cancer (oral, cervical, breast), diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis; cervical cancer screening with VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid).

---

## 6.6 Disease surveillance

**Surveillance** is the ongoing systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and timely dissemination of health data for public health action.

**Types**:
- **Passive surveillance**: health workers report cases spontaneously (using case report forms, weekly returns); depends on health workers' initiative; most common system.
- **Active surveillance**: public health staff actively seek out cases by visiting health facilities, reviewing records, or surveying communities; more sensitive but expensive.
- **Sentinel surveillance**: designate specific health facilities as sentinel sites for intensive monitoring of specific diseases (e.g. influenza-like illness, HIV sentinel surveillance in antenatal clinics).

**IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme)**: India's national disease surveillance network. Weekly reporting using three forms:
- **S-form (suspected)**: reported by community health workers and community members.
- **P-form (probable)**: reported by clinicians.
- **L-form (laboratory confirmed)**: reported by laboratories.
Data flows from facility → district → state → national (NCDC — National Centre for Disease Control).

**Notifiable diseases**: diseases that health facilities are legally required to report to health authorities. Examples: cholera, plague, smallpox, yellow fever (international); tuberculosis, malaria, dengue, kala-azar, viral encephalitis (national/state notification in India).

---

## 6.7 Outbreak investigation

An **outbreak** (epidemic) is the occurrence of disease cases in excess of what would normally be expected in a defined community, geographical area, or season.

A **pandemic** is a worldwide epidemic.

### Steps in outbreak investigation

```text
1. Verify the diagnosis (confirm cases are real; not a reporting artifact).
2. Confirm the existence of an outbreak (compare with baseline; are numbers unusual?).
3. Define a case definition (clinical + epidemiological criteria for inclusion).
4. Count cases (apply case definition to find all cases).
5. Determine descriptive epidemiology: person (who), place (where), time (when — epidemic curve).
6. Develop hypotheses about the source, mode of transmission, and risk factors.
7. Test hypotheses (analytical epidemiology — case-control or cohort study within the outbreak).
8. Implement control measures (should start early, even before all steps are complete).
9. Communicate findings to health authorities.
10. Write a report.
```

### Epidemic curve

An **epidemic curve** (epi curve) is a histogram of cases over time. The shape provides clues to the source and mode of spread:

```text
   Point source (all cases exposed at one time, e.g. contaminated food at a party):
   → Sharp peak, narrow curve (bell-shaped or single peak), cases within one incubation period
   
   Propagated (person-to-person spread, e.g. measles):
   → Progressive rise with multiple waves, each one incubation period apart
   
   Continuous source (ongoing exposure to contaminated water):
   → Extended plateau without a clear peak
```

**Incubation period** from the epidemic curve: measure from the exposure point to the peak of the curve; this indicates the most likely causative agent.

**Attack rate table**: list all persons exposed; mark who became ill; calculate attack rate by food item (or other exposure) — highest attack rate in those who ate that food item identifies the vehicle.

### Control measures

| Type | Measures |
| --- | --- |
| Source | Remove or treat the source (condemn contaminated food, treat infected persons, chlorinate water supply) |
| Route of transmission | Interrupt transmission (boil water, improve sanitation, quarantine/isolation) |
| Susceptible host | Reduce susceptibility (mass vaccination, prophylactic treatment, education) |

**Quarantine**: restriction of movement of well persons who may have been exposed to a communicable disease, for the duration of the incubation period.

**Isolation**: separation of persons known to be infected with a communicable disease from those who are not infected.

# Unit 7: Communicable diseases and national health programmes

India carries a double burden — persistent endemic communicable diseases alongside a rising NCD load. The national health programmes (vertical and integrated) are the main vehicles for controlling communicable disease. The community health nurse is a key implementer of these programmes at the field level.

---

## 7.1 Concepts of communicable disease control

**Communicable disease**: a disease caused by an infectious agent (or its toxins) that can be transmitted directly or indirectly from one person, animal, or the environment to another.

**Chain of infection**:
```text
   Infectious agent → Reservoir → Portal of exit → Mode of transmission →
   Portal of entry → Susceptible host
```

Breaking any link breaks transmission. Nursing interventions target every link (treat the source, improve sanitation, vaccinate, improve immunity).

**Incubation period**: time from exposure to first symptom. Guides quarantine duration.

**Communicability period**: period during which the infected person can transmit the disease. May overlap with or follow the incubation period.

---

## 7.2 Tuberculosis (TB) and Revised National TB Control Programme / National TB Elimination Programme

**Tuberculosis** is caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. India accounts for about 26% of global TB burden; the target is to eliminate TB (< 1 case per million population) by 2025.

**Transmission**: airborne droplet nuclei; a person with active pulmonary TB can infect 10–15 people per year if untreated.

**Diagnosis**: sputum smear microscopy (most common), GeneXpert/CBNAAT (rapid molecular diagnosis; detects rifampicin resistance within 2 hours), chest X-ray, tuberculin skin test (Mantoux), IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay for latent TB).

**Treatment categories and regimens** (NTEP 2019 onwards):

| Category | Cases | Regimen | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New cases | New pulmonary/extrapulmonary (not previously treated) | 2HRZE + 4HR (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) | 6 months |
| Previously treated | Retreatment (relapse, failure, default) | 2HRZES + HRZE + 5HRE | 8 months (or individualised per DST) |
| Drug-resistant TB (MDR, XDR) | Resistance to isoniazid + rifampicin (MDR) or more (XDR) | Longer regimen with second-line drugs (bedaquiline, linezolid, delamanid) | 9–24 months |

**DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course)**: patient takes medication under direct observation of a treatment supporter (ASHA, ANM, or community volunteer). Ensures adherence; prevents drug resistance.

**NTEP key features**: free diagnosis and treatment; electronic nikshay portal (register all TB patients, monitor treatment); Nikshay Poshan Yojana (₹500/month food support to TB patients); TB-free India by 2025 target.

**Nursing role**: contact tracing (examine household contacts for symptoms; sputum test/X-ray); promote DOTS; manage side effects (isoniazid → peripheral neuropathy → pyridoxine supplementation; rifampicin → orange discolouration of secretions — reassure); ensure nutritional support; address stigma.

---

## 7.3 Malaria

**Causative agents**: *Plasmodium falciparum* (severe disease, most deaths), *P. vivax* (most common in India, relapses), *P. malariae*, *P. ovale*.

**Vector**: *Anopheles* mosquito (female, bites dusk to dawn).

**Features**: fever with chills and rigors (every 48 hours for P. vivax, irregular for P. falciparum), headache, myalgia, hepatosplenomegaly.

**Severe malaria features** (P. falciparum): cerebral malaria (coma), severe anaemia, renal failure, respiratory failure, hypoglycaemia, blackwater fever (haemoglobinuria). Requires IV artesunate and ICU care.

**Diagnosis**: peripheral blood smear (thick and thin); rapid diagnostic test (RDT); RDT is used at village level by ASHA/MPW.

**Treatment** (NVBDCP — National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme):
- Uncomplicated P. falciparum: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) — Artesunate + Sulphadoxine-Pyrimethamine (AS+SP), 3 days.
- P. vivax: Chloroquine 25 mg/kg over 3 days + Primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day for 14 days (radical cure — after G6PD test).
- Severe malaria: IV artesunate; referral to hospital.

**NVBDCP prevention**: Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) with insecticides; Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLIN); environmental management (elimination of breeding sites); biological control (*Gambusia* fish; Bti larvicide); early diagnosis and prompt treatment (EDPT).

---

## 7.4 Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika

**Dengue**: caused by DENV 1–4 (four serotypes); vector is *Aedes aegypti* and *Ae. albopictus* (day-biting). Classic features: sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia, rash. Dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF): plasma leakage, thrombocytopenia (< 100,000/µL), haemorrhage. Dengue shock syndrome: shock from severe plasma leakage. Treatment: supportive (paracetamol, avoid aspirin/NSAIDs, IV fluids for DHF); no antiviral.

**Chikungunya**: alphavirus; *Aedes* vector; features: acute joint pain (arthralgia) often persistent months after fever resolves; no specific treatment.

**Zika**: flavivirus; *Aedes* vector; most cases mild; risk in pregnancy: microcephaly and other congenital defects.

**Prevention** (all three): reduce *Aedes* breeding sites — drain, cover, or clean water storage containers weekly; introduce *Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis* (Bti) in containers; use repellents and long sleeves; screen windows; use mosquito nets.

---

## 7.5 Lymphatic filariasis

**Causative organism**: *Wuchereria bancrofti* (most of India); vector: *Culex quinquefasciatus* (night-biting).

**Features**: acute lymphangitis, lymphadenitis; chronic: lymphoedema (elephantiasis of lower limbs), hydrocele, chyluria.

**National Filaria Control Programme**: Mass Drug Administration (MDA) annually — Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) + Albendazole to the entire at-risk population (not infected, not pregnant, not children < 2 years, not seriously ill); repeat annually for 5 years to interrupt transmission (microfilariae are killed; adult worms outlive DEC but die eventually).

**Morbidity management**: lymphoedema management education (foot hygiene, skin care, exercise, elevation, compression bandaging); hydrocele surgery.

---

## 7.6 Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis)

**Causative organism**: *Leishmania donovani*; vector: **sandfly** (*Phlebotomus argentipes*), night-biting.

**Features**: prolonged fever, progressive weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly (massive splenomegaly), anaemia, weakness; can be fatal untreated.

**Endemic areas in India**: Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh.

**Treatment**: Liposomal Amphotericin B (single IV dose under NVBDCP); Miltefosine (oral, 28 days; CI in pregnancy); Sodium Stibogluconate (SSG) — older agent.

**Prevention**: IRS (DDT or synthetic pyrethroids); bed nets (sandfly is small enough to pass through 0.25 mm mesh — fine mesh net or insecticide-treated net needed); avoid sandfly bites (peak biting: sunset to midnight).

**Elimination target**: < 1 case per 10,000 population at block level in India.

---

## 7.7 HIV/AIDS and National AIDS Control Programme (NACP)

**National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)**: the nodal government agency for India's response to HIV/AIDS under NACP.

**NACP IV key strategies**:
- **Prevention**: condom promotion, Targeted Interventions (TI) for high-risk groups (sex workers, MSM, IDUs, truckers), prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), blood safety.
- **Treatment**: free ART through government ART centres; first-line ART — TDF + 3TC + EFV (or DTG for new patients).
- **Testing**: free voluntary counselling and testing (ICTC — Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre); HIV testing integrated into ANC (opt-out for pregnant women).
- **Community mobilisation**: ASHA, NGOs, peer educators.

**Key indicators**: India has 2.4 million PLHIV (people living with HIV); national adult HIV prevalence ~0.22% (National AIDS Control Organisation estimate); 95-95-95 target (95% know status, 95% on ART, 95% virally suppressed).

---

## 7.8 Other key communicable diseases

| Disease | Agent | Mode of transmission | Key nursing action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cholera | *Vibrio cholerae* | Faecal-oral (contaminated water/food) | ORS; IV fluids for severe dehydration; notify; safe water and sanitation |
| Typhoid | *Salmonella typhi* | Faecal-oral | Antibiotic treatment (azithromycin, ciprofloxacin); identify carriers; food and water hygiene |
| Hepatitis B | HBV (blood, sexual, perinatal) | Blood, sexual contact, mother-to-child | Vaccination; safe injection practices; PEP with HBIg + vaccine for newborn of HBsAg-positive mother |
| Leptospirosis | *Leptospira* spp. | Contact with water or soil contaminated with animal urine; common after floods | Avoid flood water; protective footwear; doxycycline prophylaxis; notify |
| Rabies | Rabies virus | Animal bite (dog, bat, fox) | Wound wash (soap + water × 15 min); anti-rabies vaccination (Essen regimen or reduced regimen); rabies immunoglobulin for category III exposure |
| Japanese Encephalitis (JE) | Flavivirus | *Culex* mosquito bite | JE vaccination (endemic states); vector control; notify; supportive care |
| Plague | *Yersinia pestis* | Flea bite (bubonic), respiratory (pneumonic), direct contact (septicaemic) | Notify; isolation; doxycycline or streptomycin treatment; flea and rodent control |

---

## 7.9 National health programmes for communicable diseases

| Programme | Nodal agency | Target condition | Key activity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) | Central TB Division, MoHFW | Tuberculosis | DOTS; GeneXpert testing; Nikshay portal; free drugs |
| National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) | MoHFW | Malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filaria, kala-azar, JE | IRS; LLINs; MDA; ACT; RDT |
| National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) | NACO | HIV/AIDS | Free ART; PMTCT; targeted interventions; blood safety |
| National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) | MoHFW | Leprosy | Free MDT (rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine); disability prevention |
| Pulse Polio Programme (now part of NPSP) | MoHFW / WHO | Poliomyelitis | OPV on National Immunisation Day; AFP surveillance; India certified polio-free 2014 |
| National Immunisation Programme | MoHFW | Vaccine-preventable diseases | Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP); Mission Indradhanush |

# Unit 8: Non-communicable diseases and national health programmes

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) — cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory disease — now account for over 60% of deaths in India. The community health nurse plays a vital role in screening, early detection, lifestyle counselling, and linking people to care. This shift from acute to chronic disease is one of the defining challenges of modern public health.

---

## 8.1 Global and Indian burden of NCDs

NCDs are characterised by:
- Chronic course (lasting months to years).
- Complex, multifactorial causation.
- Largely preventable through behaviour and environment change.
- Requiring long-term management, not a single cure.

**Four main NCDs** (WHO): cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), cancers, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes mellitus. Together they account for 71% of global deaths.

**India-specific burden**: cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death; India has the second-highest number of people with diabetes globally; cancer incidence is rising, especially breast, cervical, and oral; COPD and asthma are highly prevalent due to tobacco use and air pollution.

**Common risk factors (shared across NCDs)**:
- Tobacco use.
- Harmful use of alcohol.
- Unhealthy diet (high in salt, sugar, saturated fat; low in fruits and vegetables).
- Physical inactivity.
- Overweight and obesity.
- Air pollution (indoor and outdoor).

---

## 8.2 Hypertension

**Definition**: Blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg on two separate occasions.

**Classification** (JNC 8 / India):
- Normal: < 120/80.
- Pre-hypertension: 120–139/80–89.
- Stage 1 HTN: 140–159/90–99.
- Stage 2 HTN: ≥ 160/≥ 100.

**Risk factors**: age (> 55 males, > 65 females), family history, salt intake, obesity, alcohol, sedentary lifestyle, tobacco.

**Complications**: stroke, coronary artery disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, retinopathy.

**Screening**: CPHC guidelines recommend screening all adults ≥ 30 years at HWCs; take BP in both arms first time; confirm on 2 separate visits.

**Community nursing role**:
- Measure BP accurately (cuff size, sitting, after 5 minutes rest, no caffeine or smoking within 30 minutes).
- Lifestyle counselling: DASH diet (reduce salt to < 5 g/day, increase fruits and vegetables, reduce saturated fat, limit alcohol); weight reduction; physical activity (150 min/week moderate intensity); smoking cessation.
- Medication adherence support; identify side effects (cough with ACE inhibitors, ankle oedema with amlodipine, impotence with β-blockers).
- Home BP monitoring; keep a BP diary.

---

## 8.3 Diabetes mellitus

**Type 1**: autoimmune destruction of β-cells; insulin-dependent; onset usually in childhood/young adults; thin; 10–15% of all diabetes.

**Type 2**: insulin resistance + progressive β-cell failure; linked to obesity and lifestyle; 85–90% of cases; most adults at community level.

**Gestational diabetes**: onset or first detected during pregnancy; risk of complications for mother and baby; reverts in most cases but high risk of T2DM later.

**Diagnosis criteria** (WHO/IDF):
- FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) on two occasions, OR
- 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL after OGTT, OR
- HbA1c ≥ 6.5%, OR
- Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with symptoms.

**Screening**: CPHC protocol — fasting blood glucose using glucometer at HWCs for all adults ≥ 30 years.

**Management goals**: HbA1c < 7% (< 53 mmol/mol); BP < 130/80; LDL < 2.6 mmol/L.

**Lifestyle management**: dietary advice (consistent carbohydrate intake; limit refined sugar and white rice; increase fibre; portion control); physical activity 150 min/week; weight management; smoking cessation; foot care (inspect feet daily, never walk barefoot, appropriate footwear, nail care, check for numbness — diabetic neuropathy).

**Community nursing role**:
- Screen and refer new diagnoses.
- Medication adherence (oral hypoglycaemic agents: metformin, sulfonylureas; insulin).
- Monitor for complications (retinopathy → annual eye check; nephropathy → urine albumin/creatinine ratio; neuropathy → foot exam; CVD risk).
- Hypoglycaemia recognition and management (< 70 mg/dL: fast-acting glucose, then complex carbohydrate; unconscious: glucagon injection or IV dextrose; teach family members).
- Self-monitoring of blood glucose education.

---

## 8.4 Cardiovascular diseases

**Coronary artery disease (CAD)**: narrowing of coronary arteries by atherosclerosis → angina, MI. Major modifiable risk factors: hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, smoking, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet.

**Stroke**: sudden onset neurological deficit from cerebral infarction (ischaemic, 85%) or haemorrhage (15%). Risk factors: same as CAD plus atrial fibrillation, oral contraceptive use in smokers.

**Rehabilitation after MI/stroke**: community nurse role in home rehabilitation, medication adherence (aspirin, statins, antihypertensives), lifestyle counselling, family education, psychosocial support (depression is common after both), and preventing recurrence.

**Rheumatic fever / Rheumatic heart disease (RHD)**: untreated Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → autoimmune damage to heart valves. India has high RHD burden. Prevention: prompt treatment of strep throat with penicillin; secondary prophylaxis (monthly benzathine penicillin injections for 5–10 years to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever).

---

## 8.5 Cancer

**Leading cancers in India by incidence** (ICMR 2022): breast (women), cervical (women), oral/lip (men), lung, colorectal, stomach, leukaemia.

**Warning signs of cancer (CAUTION)**:
- Change in bowel or bladder habits.
- A sore that does not heal.
- Unusual bleeding or discharge.
- Thickening or lump in breast or elsewhere.
- Indigestion or difficulty in swallowing.
- Obvious change in a wart or mole.
- Nagging cough or hoarseness.

**Breast cancer screening**: clinical breast examination (CBE) every 3 years for women 25–39, annually from 40; mammography for high-risk women; breast self-examination (BSE) — teach women to examine breasts monthly after menstruation.

**Cervical cancer screening**: Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) — cotton swab soaked in 3–5% acetic acid applied to cervix; acetowhite areas indicate HPV-infected or pre-cancerous cells; widely used in India at PHC level by trained ANMs. HPV vaccination: Gardasil/Cervarix for girls 9–14 years; reduces risk of cervical cancer.

**Oral cancer screening**: examine the oral cavity for white patches (leukoplakia), red patches (erythroplakia), non-healing ulcers, abnormal lumps; risk factors: tobacco (smoking and smokeless), alcohol, betel nut. Oral visual examination done by ASHA, ANM, or health worker.

**Community nursing role**: teach cancer warning signs; conduct CBE and oral examination during home visits and outreach camps; promote VIA screening; support newly diagnosed patients and their families; facilitate access to cancer treatment (referral to district cancer care unit or tertiary centre); pain management and palliative care in advanced disease.

---

## 8.6 Chronic respiratory diseases

**Asthma**: reversible airway obstruction due to inflammation and hyper-reactivity. Management: inhaled bronchodilators (β₂ agonists — salbutamol for acute relief) + inhaled corticosteroids (ICS — for maintenance); avoid triggers.

**COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease)**: progressive, largely irreversible obstruction; caused mainly by smoking and biomass fuel smoke; characterised by chronic cough, sputum, and dyspnoea; FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 on spirometry. Management: smoking cessation (most important); bronchodilators (long-acting β₂ agonists and/or anticholinergics); ICS for frequent exacerbations; pulmonary rehabilitation; oxygen therapy for severe disease.

**Nurse's role**: spirometry performance; smoking cessation counselling; correct inhaler technique (a common problem — patients use spacer devices incorrectly); exacerbation recognition (increased dyspnoea, purulent sputum → start antibiotics/prednisolone); nutrition support; psychosocial support.

---

## 8.7 Mental health and national programmes

**Common mental disorders in the community**: depression, anxiety, alcohol and substance use disorders (high prevalence, low treatment rates).

**Suicide**: India accounts for over 17% of global suicides; adolescents and farmers are high-risk groups; underlying mental illness (depression, substance use) in most cases. The nurse's role: safe messaging (do not glamorise); risk assessment; listening without judgement; refer to mental health professional; remove access to means where possible.

**National Mental Health Programme (NMHP)**: District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) — trained mental health teams at district level; integration of mental health into primary health care (mhGAP — Mental Health Gap Action Programme: trained primary care staff to identify and treat common mental disorders with WHO mhGAP guide).

**Alcohol and substance use**: India has high alcohol use disorder burden; tobacco use (smoking and smokeless tobacco); cannabis, opioids (especially in Northeast). Intervention: brief motivational counselling; referral to deaddiction centres; Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan (National NCD awareness programme for youth).

---

## 8.8 National NCD programme

**National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease and Stroke (NPCDCS)**: India's main NCD control programme.

**Key activities under NPCDCS**:
- Population-based screening at HWCs for hypertension, diabetes, three common cancers (oral, breast, cervical) for all persons ≥ 30 years.
- NCD clinics at CHC level.
- Cardiac care units and cancer care units at district level.
- Lifestyle modification counselling (CPHC wellness activities).
- Referral pathways from community to district.

**Community Health Officer (CHO) at HWC**: performs population-level NCD screening; provides basic treatment for common conditions; counsels on lifestyle change; refers complex cases to PHC or higher.

**Tobacco control**: National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP); COTPA 2003 (Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act) — prohibits tobacco advertisements, mandates graphic warning labels, bans smoking in public places; National Quitline (1800-11-2356); mCessation text-message programme.

**Nurse's advocacy role in NCD prevention**: conduct NCD screening camps; support self-help groups for diabetes and hypertension (peer support improves adherence); promote physical activity in community settings (yoga, walking groups); advocate for smoke-free environments and healthy school canteens; support policy (salt and sugar reduction in food; trans-fat elimination); address the mental health dimension of living with chronic disease.
